overview.title: Limits of subclassed models; mixing model-building styles
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: What Model subclassing gains and loses compared with the Functional API, and how the three model-building styles interoperate
overview.central_idea: A subclassed model is arbitrary Python code rather than an inspectable graph of layers: that buys unlimited flexibility (loops, recursion) at the cost of debugging burden, summary()/plot_model() connectivity, and feature extraction. None of this locks you in, because Sequential, Functional and subclassed components can be freely nested inside each other.
overview.importance: This page is the hinge between learning the three model-building APIs and choosing among them (p.229). Understanding why a Functional model can be inspected while a subclassed one cannot explains the book's recommendation to default to the Functional API with subclassed layers inside it (p.230).
learning_objectives: Run evaluate() and predict() on a multi-input, multi-output subclassed model with the correct input and output structures
Explain why subclassing can express models that are not directed acyclic graphs of layers
List the concrete features lost with subclassed models: layer connectivity in summary(), plot_model(), and access to intermediate graph nodes for feature extraction
Contrast a Functional model (explicit data structure) with a subclassed model (bytecode inside call())
State that Sequential, Functional and subclassed models/layers interoperate, and recognize the start of Listing 7.15
prerequisites: The CustomerTicketModel subclass and its compile()/fit() calls (p.226-227)
The Functional API and its access to layer connectivity (p.219, p.223)

summary:
The page opens by finishing the `CustomerTicketModel` example from p.226-227. After compiling and fitting the subclassed model, you call `model.evaluate()` with the same dict of three inputs (`title`, `text_body`, `tags`) and the list of two targets (`priority_data`, `department_data`), and `model.predict()` with just the input dict, which returns a pair of arrays that unpack into `priority_preds` and `department_preds`. The structures must match what `call()` consumes and returns.

The authors then step back. **Model subclassing is the most flexible workflow**: since the forward pass is ordinary Python, it can express models that are *not* directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of layers, for example a `call()` that applies layers in a `for` loop or calls them recursively.

The sidebar **"Beware: What subclassed models don't support"** lists the price:

- You own more of the model logic, so the *error surface* is larger and you will debug more: "you are developing a new Python object, not just snapping together LEGO bricks."
- A Functional model is an **explicit data structure**, a graph of layers you can view, inspect and modify. A subclassed model is **bytecode**: a class whose `call()` contains raw code.
- Because connectivity lives inside `call()`, Keras cannot see it. `summary()` will not show how layers connect, `plot_model()` cannot draw the topology, and you cannot reach intermediate nodes for **feature extraction**, "because there is simply no graph." After instantiation the forward pass is a **black box**.

Section **7.2.4** then makes the reassuring point that picking one pattern doesn't lock you out of the others. Sequential models, Functional models and subclassed models or layers all interoperate as parts of one *spectrum of workflows* (p.215). The first example is a subclassed component used inside a Functional model. **Listing 7.15** begins here with `class Classifier(keras.Model)` and its `__init__(self, num_classes=2)` calling `super().__init__()`. The rest of the listing, which chooses sigmoid or softmax and wires the class into a Functional graph, is on p.229.

paragraphs.excerpt: The Model subclassing workflow is the most flexible way to build a model
paragraphs.what_it_says: Subclassing is the most flexible way to build a model. It can express models that are not DAGs of layers, such as a call() that uses layers inside a for loop or calls them recursively. 'Anything is possible—you're in charge.'
paragraphs.what_it_means: The Functional API can only build what can be written as a static graph from inputs to outputs, with each layer call producing a node. A subclassed model's call() is plain Python, so the computation can depend on Python control flow: a loop whose length is a hyperparameter or depends on the data, a recursive call over a tree-shaped input, or branching on a flag.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the one real reason to choose subclassing over the Functional API. The next page (p.229) recommends the Functional API whenever the model *can* be expressed as a DAG.
paragraphs.technical_idea: DAG = directed acyclic graph. Functional models are DAGs of layer calls, so cycles (true recursion) and data-dependent structure can't be written directly. Python code in call() has no such restriction. Beyond the book: under the JAX or TensorFlow backends, compiled execution still constrains data-dependent control flow, but the model definition itself is unrestricted.

terminology.meaning: A graph whose edges have a direction and that contains no cycles; Functional models are DAGs whose nodes are layer outputs.
A function (here, a forward pass) that calls itself, e.g. applying the same layer repeatedly over a nested structure.

connections: p.226: the subclassing recipe (layers in __init__, forward pass in call())
p.229: recommendation to prefer the Functional API when a DAG suffices

paragraphs.excerpt: This freedom comes at a cost: with subclassed models, you are responsible
paragraphs.what_it_says: With subclassed models you are responsible for more of the model logic, so the potential error surface is much larger and you will do more debugging. You are developing a new Python object, not snapping together LEGO bricks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In the Functional API Keras checks a lot for you as you build: every layer call is shape-checked against its input when the graph is constructed, and mistakes show up immediately at the line that caused them. In a subclassed model, errors only appear when call() actually runs on data, and any bug in your Python (a wrong variable, a layer used twice by accident, a forgotten argument) is yours to find.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the trade-off honestly: flexibility is not free, and the cost is paid in engineering time and correctness risk.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The LEGO metaphor echoes p.219, where the Functional API is said to 'feel like playing with LEGO bricks'.

terminology.meaning: The set of places where bugs can live; more hand-written logic means more such places.

connections: p.219: Functional API compared to LEGO bricks
p.216: subclassing described as putting you 'more at risk of making mistakes'

paragraphs.excerpt: Functional and subclassed models are also substantially different in nature: a Functional
paragraphs.what_it_says: A Functional model is an explicit data structure, a graph of layers you can view, inspect and modify. A subclassed model is a piece of bytecode: a Python class whose call() method contains raw code. That is where its flexibility comes from, but it brings new limitations.
paragraphs.what_it_means: When you build a Functional model, Keras records every layer call as a node with known inputs and outputs, and the model object stores this graph. When you subclass Model, Keras only knows which layers you assigned as attributes in __init__ (so it can track their weights). How they are chained exists only as Python instructions that run when call() executes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This difference in kind explains every limitation in the next paragraph. Tools that need the graph have nothing to read.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Data structure vs. code: a graph can be traversed (model.layers, layer.input/output, model.get_layer(...).output). Code can only be executed.

terminology.meaning: Compiled Python instructions; here, shorthand for 'opaque executable code' as opposed to an inspectable data structure.
An object whose structure (nodes and edges) is stored and queryable.

connections: p.223: 'A Functional model is an explicit graph data structure'

paragraphs.excerpt: For instance, because the way layers are connected to each other is
paragraphs.what_it_says: Since connectivity is hidden in call(), you can't access it. summary() won't show layer connectivity, plot_model() can't plot the topology, and you can't reach the nodes of the layer graph for feature extraction, because there is no graph. Once instantiated, the forward pass is a complete black box.
paragraphs.what_it_means: summary() on a subclassed model lists the tracked sublayers and their parameter counts, but not which layer feeds which. plot_model() has no edges to draw. The feature-extraction trick from p.223-224, building `keras.Model(inputs=model.inputs, outputs=model.get_layer("...").output)`, needs symbolic intermediate tensors, and a subclassed model has none.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Visualization and feature extraction were presented on p.223 as the two major payoffs of the Functional API. This paragraph states that subclassing gives both up.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Feature extraction = reusing intermediate activations of an existing model as outputs of a new model. Beyond the book: with a subclassed model you'd have to change call() itself to return the intermediate values.

terminology.meaning: Building a new model whose outputs are intermediate layer outputs of an existing model.
keras.utils.plot_model, which renders a model's layer graph as an image.
Something whose internal structure is not observable from outside; only inputs and outputs are visible.

connections: p.223: model visualization and feature extraction as uses of layer connectivity
p.224: reusing intermediate layer outputs in a new model

paragraphs.excerpt: Crucially, choosing one of these patterns—the Sequential model, the Functional API, Model
paragraphs.what_it_says: Choosing Sequential, Functional or subclassing doesn't lock you out of the others. All Keras models interoperate smoothly; they belong to one spectrum of workflows. For example, you can use a subclassed layer or model in a Functional model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Every one of these objects is a Layer under the hood: a Model is a Layer that also has fit()/evaluate()/predict() (p.227). Anything that is a Layer can be called on a symbolic tensor inside a Functional graph, or assigned as an attribute and called inside another class's call(). So you can confine the 'black box' to a small custom component and keep the rest of the model an inspectable graph.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It removes the all-or-nothing choice. The practical pattern recommended on p.230, Functional models containing subclassed layers, follows from this.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Composability is possible because of the shared base classes Layer and Model (p.215). Beyond the book: inside a Functional graph, a subclassed component appears as a single node; its internals stay opaque but its inputs and outputs are visible.

terminology.meaning: Work together; here, nest freely as building blocks of each other.
The book's term (p.215) for Keras's range of APIs from simple to fully custom, all built on shared APIs.

connections: p.215: all workflows share the Layer and Model APIs and can talk to each other
p.229: the reverse direction, a Functional model inside a subclassed model (Listing 7.16)
p.230: Functional models with subclassed layers give 'the best of both worlds'

concepts.name: Model subclassing
concepts.definition: Building a model by inheriting from keras.Model, creating layers in __init__() and writing the forward pass in call().
concepts.intuition: You write the model as a program instead of describing it as a diagram.
concepts.technical: Keras tracks sublayers assigned as attributes (for weights and saving), but the connectivity is whatever call() computes at run time. No symbolic graph is stored.
concepts.significance: It's the most flexible way to build models (loops, recursion, non-DAG logic), but you lose graph-based tooling and take on more debugging.
concepts.misconception: That subclassed models can't use fit()/evaluate()/predict(). They can, exactly like Functional models, as the code at the top of this page shows.

concepts.name: Functional API
concepts.definition: The Keras style in which models are built by calling layers on symbolic tensors, producing an explicit graph of layers.
concepts.intuition: A wiring diagram Keras can read, draw and rewire.
concepts.technical: The model stores nodes (layer outputs) and edges, which makes summary() connectivity, plot_model(), and reusing intermediate outputs possible.
concepts.significance: The book's recommended default whenever the model is a DAG of layers (p.229-230).
concepts.example: keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs) built from keras.Input and layer calls.
concepts.misconception: That the Functional API can't contain custom code. It can include subclassed layers or models as nodes (Listing 7.15).

concepts.name: Directed acyclic graph of layers
concepts.definition: A layer topology where data flows from inputs to outputs along directed edges without cycles.
concepts.intuition: Water flowing downhill through pipes: it can split and merge but never loops back.
concepts.technical: Any model where each layer call's inputs are earlier outputs fits; recursion or data-dependent repetition does not fit as a static DAG.
concepts.significance: The boundary between what the Functional API can express and what needs subclassing.
concepts.example: Multi-input, multi-output ticket classifier (p.222) is a DAG; a recursive tree network is not.
concepts.misconception: That 'non-sequential' means 'non-DAG'. Branches and merges are still DAGs.

concepts.name: Feature extraction (from intermediate layers)
concepts.definition: Building a new model that outputs the activations of intermediate layers of an existing model.
concepts.intuition: Tapping into the pipes in the middle of the wiring diagram.
concepts.technical: It requires access to symbolic intermediate tensors (layer.output), which exist only for graph-based (Functional/Sequential) models.
concepts.significance: One of the two key capabilities the book says subclassed models lack.
concepts.misconception: That you can do the same on a subclassed model with get_layer(...).output. There is no graph, so no symbolic output to grab.

concepts.name: Interoperability of model-building styles
concepts.definition: Sequential models, Functional models and subclassed layers or models can be nested inside each other freely.
concepts.intuition: Different kinds of building blocks that all share the same connector.
concepts.technical: Everything subclasses Layer, so any of them can be called on tensors inside another model's graph or call().
concepts.significance: It lets you keep custom, opaque logic small and local while the overall model stays inspectable.
concepts.example: Listing 7.15: a subclassed Classifier model used as a layer in a Functional model.
concepts.misconception: That once you subclass anything, the whole model loses Functional features. Only the subclassed part becomes a single opaque node.

code.title: Evaluating and predicting with the subclassed CustomerTicketModel
code.what_it_does: Evaluates the trained subclassed model on inputs and targets, then runs inference to get predictions for both heads. It is the end of the snippet that starts with compile() and fit() on p.227.

line_explanations.explanation: evaluate() takes inputs as a dict keyed by the names call() reads ("title", "text_body", "tags") and targets as a list in the same order call() returns its outputs (priority, then department). It returns the total loss plus per-output losses and metrics configured in compile().

predict() takes only the input dict and returns the model's outputs, here a pair of NumPy arrays that unpack into priority_preds (shape (n, 1), sigmoid score) and department_preds (shape (n, num_departments), softmax probabilities).

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: title_data, text_body_data, tags_data (the multi-input data used for the ticket model earlier in 7.2); targets priority_data, department_data. Outputs: evaluation results; two prediction arrays.
code.algorithm: Batch the inputs, run call() forward on each batch, and for evaluate() compute losses/metrics against targets.
code.theory_link: Shows that subclassed models plug into the same built-in loops as Functional models (p.227).

parameters.name: inputs dict
parameters.role: Must match the keys call() reads from inputs.

parameters.name: targets list
parameters.role: Must match the order and number of outputs returned by call().

pitfalls: Passing targets as a dict or in the wrong order when call() returns a list or tuple: structures must match exactly (p.227 callouts).
Forgetting that predict() returns a tuple/list here, not a single array.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: inspect what evaluate returns
results = model.evaluate(
    {"title": title_data, "text_body": text_body_data, "tags": tags_data},
    [priority_data, department_data],
    return_dict=True,
)
print(results)  # total loss, per-output losses, and per-output metrics
print(priority_preds.shape, department_preds.shape)

deeper.title: What a non-DAG model looks like
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: two examples of what the first paragraph means.

1. **Repeated application**: `for _ in range(self.num_steps): x = self.block(x)` reuses *one* layer `num_steps` times. Shared weights in a loop amount to a recurrence, and the loop count can be a call-time argument.
2. **Recursion**: a model over parse trees that calls `self.combine(self(left), self(right))` until it reaches leaves. The structure differs per input, so no single static graph describes it.

In the Functional API you would have to unroll a fixed number of steps by hand, and the second case can't be written at all.

deeper.title: Blueprint vs. recipe
deeper.body: A Functional model is like an architect's **blueprint**: anyone can read off which room connects to which, print it (plot_model), or build a new house from half of it (feature extraction). A subclassed model is like a **recipe written as free-form instructions**: you can follow it and get the dish, but nobody can extract 'the intermediate sauce' unless the author changes the recipe to set some aside.

deeper.title: What summary() shows for each style
deeper.body:
Beyond the book (typical Keras 3 behaviour):

- **Functional**: one row per layer, with output shapes and, for multi-input models, a column showing which layers it is *connected to*.
- **Subclassed**: one row per tracked sublayer with parameter counts. Output shapes may be unknown until the model is called, and there is no connectivity information, which matches the book's statement.

Try it: build the ticket model both ways (p.222 and p.226) and compare `model.summary()`.

misconceptions.claim: Subclassed models are 'more powerful' so they should be the default.
misconceptions.correction: They're more flexible, but they cost you debugging effort, connectivity in summary(), plot_model() and feature extraction. The book recommends the Functional API whenever the model is a DAG of layers (p.229).

misconceptions.claim: Once you write one custom subclassed piece, your whole model must be subclassed.
misconceptions.correction: All styles interoperate. A subclassed layer or model can sit inside a Functional model (Listing 7.15), and a Functional model can sit inside a subclassed one (Listing 7.16, p.229).

misconceptions.claim: summary() doesn't work on subclassed models.
misconceptions.correction: It works, but it doesn't display layer connectivity, because that information is hidden in call().

misconceptions.claim: Subclassed models can't be trained with fit()/evaluate()/predict().
misconceptions.correction: They can. The top of this page evaluates and predicts with a subclassed model, after compile() and fit() on p.227.

takeaways: Subclassed models support evaluate() and predict() with the same input/target structure rules as fit().
Subclassing can express non-DAG models (loops, recursion) that the Functional API cannot.
The cost is more of your own logic to debug, plus no connectivity in summary(), no plot_model() topology and no intermediate-node feature extraction.

questions.question: Which of the following can you NOT do with a subclassed Keras model, according to this page?
options: Plot its layer topology with plot_model()
questions.answer: Plot its layer topology with plot_model()
questions.explanation: Connectivity is hidden inside call(), so plot_model() has no graph to draw. fit() and predict() work (p.227 and the code here), and summary() runs but doesn't show connectivity.

questions.question: Give an example from the page of a model that cannot be expressed as a directed acyclic graph of layers.
questions.answer: A model whose call() uses layers inside a for loop, or calls them recursively.
questions.explanation: Both examples are given in the first paragraph. Such data- or argument-dependent structure isn't a static DAG.

questions.question: Why can't you do feature extraction on a subclassed model the way you can on a Functional model?
questions.answer: Feature extraction reuses intermediate graph nodes (layer outputs) as outputs of a new model. A subclassed model stores no graph, only Python code in call(), so there are no intermediate nodes to access.
questions.explanation: The page states 'there is simply no graph'. Compare p.223, where the explicit graph enables reusing intermediate nodes.

questions.question: In the evaluate() call at the top of the page, why are the targets passed as a list of two arrays?
options: Because evaluate() always requires a list
Because the model's call() returns two outputs (priority, department) in that order
Because there are two input features
Because the loss is a sum of two terms that Keras cannot infer
questions.answer: Because the model's call() returns two outputs (priority, department) in that order
questions.explanation: Target structure must match what call() returns (p.227 callouts). evaluate() doesn't always need a list. The model has three inputs, not two. The two losses are configured explicitly in compile().

questions.question: Explain the difference the authors draw between a Functional model as an 'explicit data structure' and a subclassed model as 'a piece of bytecode'.
questions.answer: A Functional model stores its graph of layers, which can be viewed, inspected and modified. A subclassed model is a Python class whose call() contains raw code; how layers connect only exists when that code runs.
questions.explanation: This difference is what gives subclassing its flexibility and what causes all of its listed limitations.

questions.question: What does Listing 7.15 demonstrate?
options: A subclassed model that contains a Functional model
A Functional model that includes a subclassed model
Converting a Sequential model into a subclassed model
questions.answer: A Functional model that includes a subclassed model
questions.explanation: Its caption says so: the Classifier subclass is used as a component of a Functional model (completed on p.229). The reverse direction is Listing 7.16. The other two options aren't shown.

questions.question: Can you list three things you give up by choosing model subclassing, and say when the trade-off is worth it?
questions.answer: You give up layer connectivity in summary(), plot_model() topology and feature extraction from intermediate nodes, and you take on more debugging. It's worth it when the model genuinely can't be a DAG of layers (loops, recursion).
questions.explanation: This combines the sidebar with the first paragraph and the recommendation on p.229.
